headlines.title: Preliminary 2.9 magnitude earthquake strikes near Gilroy
headlines.description: A preliminary 2.9 magnitude earthquake struck near Gilroy Friday afternoon, according to the United States Geological Survey. The quake hit at 1:02 p.m. and was centered 7.1 miles east-southeast of Gilroy, 8.3 miles north-northwest of Hollister and 16 miles southeast of Morgan Hill, the USGS said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. BAY AREA QUAKE CENTRAL Bay Area Quake Tracker, the latest earthquake stories, extensive quake prep checklists, videos and many other disaster preparedness resources all in one place: NBCBAYAREA.COM/QUAKES

headlines.title: 1 dead, 1 injured after shooting in Oakland, sources say
headlines.description: A woman was killed and another person was injured in a shooting in Oakland Friday morning, police sources told NBC Bay Area. The shooting happened in the area of Ney Avenue and Ritchie Street. The woman died at the scene, sources said. The person who was injured was taken to the hospital. Their condition wasn’t immediately known. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates.

headlines.title: 10th annual dog surfing competition to be held Saturday in Pacifica
headlines.description: Nearly 20 different dogs, from scruffy terriers to Labrador retrievers, will show off their best surfing skills Saturday at the 10th annual World Dog Surfing Championships in Pacifica. Dogs of all different breeds and sizes will compete for the ultimate prize at Linda Mar Beach during the free event, which will run from 9 a.m. to 2 p.m. The dogs will compete in various “heats” throughout the day, categorizing dogs by size. There are also dogs participating in categories with their human partners, such as standup paddle-boarding and tandem surfing. Some returning dogs include miniature pinscher Rusty, Labrador retriever Rippin Rosie, and Carson Surf Dog. A team of judges will evaluate their performances and declare a winner from each category. Judges will score each dog based on length of ride, size of the wave, confidence, balance and extra tricks. The winners of the small, medium, and large-size categories will then go head-to-head for the grand prize. Competitors will then retreat to Puerto 27 Restaurant for an “Apres Surf” gathering until 5 p.m. It will include food, drinks, and a meet-and-greet. In the past, the competition has drawn thousands of spectators, who descend on the beach to catch a glimpse of the four-legged surfers in action.

headlines.title: 59-year-old Sunnyvale woman detained by ICE at airport in New York
headlines.description: Immigration authorities detained a 59-year-old Sunnyvale resident earlier this month and shuttled her through multiple detention centers in the days that followed, often under severe physical conditions, according to her family. Alevtina Soboleva was at the airport in Buffalo, New York, on July 20 to board a flight back to the Bay Area after a vacation at Niagara Falls when plainclothes officers approached her for a “documents check,” said Soboleva’s 30-year-old daughter Daria, who was with her at the time. At the time, the officers did not identify themselves as belonging to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement or any other immigration agency, Daria Soboleva said. Her mother was then transported from one detention facility to another, Daria Soboleva said. “There is no control in this situation with what’s happening,” she said in an interview on Thursday. “She is just moved, and I cannot find her, I cannot speak to her.” ICE records show that, as of Thursday afternoon, Alevtina is currently in custody at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center in Basile, Louisiana. She has been in detention for 10 days. ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday evening on Alevtina Soboleva’s case. Daria Soboleva, a research scientist at Sunnyvale-based firm Cerebras Systems, said that her mother moved to the United States from Russia in October 2021 to help her settle into her new job. In 2022, when war broke out between Russia and Ukraine, they decided that it was unsafe to return to Russia. In April 2022, Alevtina Soboleva filed for her asylum application, which is still pending. “She does not have any criminal record,” Daria Soboleva said Thursday. “She did everything right, and I don’t understand what has happened.” After officers took custody of Alevtina Soboleva at the Buffalo airport, her daughter could not contact her for four days. When the two finally spoke, Alevtina Soboleva had been moved to the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center. “When she was able to speak to me for the first time, she was just crying nonstop,” Daria Soboleva said. “She was so humiliated, she could never imagine being treated like this.” According to their phone conversation, Alevtina was shackled with handcuffs and chains and placed inside a cage as she was transported from one detention center to another. The cage, Alevtina recounted to Daria, had very poor air circulation, and when she asked to be let out to breathe fresh air, she was not permitted to do so. She was refused the use of a bathroom and had to urinate on herself. She also suffered panic attacks and was refused water when she asked for it. “She was begging them just to wet her lips a little because she had been there for hours,” said Daria. “That wasn’t allowed, too.” After arriving at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, she complained of chills and asked for warm clothing, but was not provided any. When a fellow detainee gave her fever medication and a warm hat, authorities at the detention center took them away from her. Now, Daria can speak with her mother but is worried about her health, given that she already suffers from vertigo. The family has engaged their attorney as well as the office of Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Santa Clara, to expedite the proceedings and bring Alevtina back home. “My mom is going through this, but I cannot imagine anyone’s mom going through this,” said Daria. “To me, it just sounds like a very, very bad nightmare.”

headlines.title: Anthropic says its AI models hacked 3 organizations during testing
headlines.description: Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, just days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI raised concerns over AI controls after it disclosed its rogue models hacked another company. Anthropic, the San Francisco-based AI company behind Claude, posted on its website Thursday that it discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs. It had launched a “large-scale” cybersecurity review which specifically looked for evidence whether its AI models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off, in response to the OpenAI incident, Anthropic said. Anthropic said the models involved in the incidents were Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model. The earliest incidents date to April, the AI company said. “Claude compromised the impacted organizations’ infrastructure using basic techniques,” Anthropic said, such as exploiting weak passwords. In all three incidents, the AI models were tasked with a “capture the flag” cybersecurity challenge, which Anthropic said has been one of the ways it assesses a model’s cyber capabilities. The models were given a fictional scenario and told a piece of secret information, or the “flag,” had been hidden on a different machine on the network with the objective of breaking in and retrieving it, it said. It added that it had already reached out to the affected organizations, which it did not name. Two of them said they had not previously detected the activity. Anthropic said it was “continuing to reach out to the third.” Anthropic said it conducted its review with Irregular, which describes itself as the “first frontier security lab.” “Addressing these risks will require closer cooperation across the AI ecosystem,” Irregular said in a post on X. Last week, OpenAI said its AI models went rogue during an evaluation of its models, breaking into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. OpenAI described it as a “significant security incident.” These incidents have highlighted the vulnerabilities in AI security and controls and raised questions over how AI can be safely kept under human control as the technology’s usage becomes more widespread globally. Researchers have warned for years about risks from technology and the need for stronger AI defensive engineering. “Safety testing happens before a model is released precisely because we don’t yet know what it is capable of,” Anthropic said on Thursday on its website. Kok Tin Gan, co-founder & CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab, which specializes in cybersecurity and threat detection, believes there will be more such incidents in the future. “It is increasingly about governing what agents are available to the AI, what authorities they possess, which actions require approval, and how we ensure they remain within scope,” Gan said. But the future of AI safety extends beyond just the safety of AI models, he said. “If we simply give the AI a goal and allow it to decide how to achieve it, we should not be surprised when it takes actions that technically satisfy the objective, but fall outside our intended scope or expectations,” Gan said. Therefore, stepping up the governance of the organizations and authorities behind these AI models is going to be increasingly important, he said.

headlines.title: Sonoma County Woodside Fire: Containment increases, Spare the Air alert extended
headlines.description: Firefighters made progress overnight on the Woodside Fire along the Sonoma County coast, increasing containment to 30 percent Friday morning as crews continued battling the wildfire near state Highway 1. A Spare the Air alert issued in the Bay Area due to the blaze was extended through Saturday, authorities announced Friday. The fire has burned about 142 acres, according to the latest update from Cal Fire. Overnight, favorable weather conditions allowed firefighters to strengthen containment, the agency said. The wildfire started about 1:45 p.m. Thursday in the 24000 block of Highway 1 near Timber Cove. There have been no reports of injuries, as of 7 a.m. Friday. Sonoma County 22 hours ago Solano County 4 hours ago bay area weather 6 hours ago More than 30 fire engines, eight hand crews, a bulldozer, eight water tenders, a fall module and overhead personnel were assigned to the fire, as of 7 a.m. Friday. Authorities urge residents to stay away from the area, so firefighters and emergency crews can continue their work safely. Highway 1 remains closed between Timber Cove Road and Stewarts Point-Skaggs Springs Road because of the fire. An evacuation order remains in effect for Zone SON-1D1, which includes Salt Point State Park, Timber Cove and nearby areas. Evacuation orders had also been issued for Stillwater Cove Regional Park, Ocean Cove Private Camp and the Timber Cove subdivision. Zone SON-1D2, northwest of Cazadero, remains under an evacuation warning. A temporary evacuation shelter remains open at Laguna High School, formerly El Molino High School, at 7050 Covey Road in Forestville. Authorities said anyone needing help evacuating pets can contact Sonoma CART, while help for livestock is available through NorCal Livestock Evac. The cause of the fire remains to be confirmed. Woodside Fire triggers Spare the Air alert The Bay Area Air District’s Spare the Air alert had gone into effect because of smoke from the fire, with unhealthy air quality expected in parts of the North Bay. During a Spare the Air alert, burning wood both indoors and outdoors becomes illegal. First-time violators can choose to take a wood smoke awareness course instead of paying a $100 fine. Ticket amounts increase with subsequent violations. Gas, propane, or electric fireplaces are allowed to run during Spare the Air Alerts. Homes where wood stoves or closed fireplaces are the sole sources of heat may qualify for an exemption. Residents can check whether a Spare the Air alert is in effect by visiting www.sparetheair.org, calling 877-466-2876, signing up for text or email alerts, or downloading the Spare the Air mobile app.

headlines.title: 3 dead after head-on crash outside Vacaville
headlines.description: Three people died Friday in a head-on crash on a rural highway outside Vacaville, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision happened at about 6:35 a.m. on Highway 113, just north of Hay Road, the CHP said. Citing a preliminary investigation and witness statements, the CHP said the driver of a red GMC pickup truck reportedly was overtaking other vehicles at a high rate of speed when they crossed into oncoming traffic and slammed head-on into a gray Ram pickup truck. The driver and passenger in the GMC pickup truck and the driver of the Ram pickup truck all died at the scene, the CHP said. Highway 113 was closed in both directions following the crash, according to the CHP. The crash remains under investigation.

headlines.title: San Jose mall to host late-night rave in September
headlines.description: A late-night rave is coming to a San Jose mall in September. The rave, billed as a takeover at Eastridge mall, is scheduled for Sept. 5 from 9 p.m. to 2 a.m. Organizers said they’re bringing a full stage, lighting and a secret lineup of DJs. Presale tickets went on sale Friday morning.

headlines.title: Family of SFO worker who died at airport files wrongful death lawsuit
headlines.description: The family of a San Francisco International Airport worker who died at the airport in January has filed a wrongful death lawsuit. The family of 28-year-old John Lacayanga is suing the city and county of San Francisco, Ground Services International, and dnata USA. On January 18, Lacayanga was found under a cargo pallet he had been towing on an airport road. It’s not clear how he ended up there. He was working for dnata at the time. Lawyers for Lacayanga’s parents said the defendants committed multiple acts of negligence and created dangerous conditions. NBC Bay Area reached out to San Francisco and the companies named in the lawsuit for a response but did not immediately hear back.

headlines.title: Californians' data deletion requests, DROP, become enforceable Aug. 1
headlines.description: If you’ve ever wondered how much of your personal information is collected every time you go online, California is giving consumers a new way to push back. Starting Aug. 1, registered California data brokers must begin honoring requests submitted through the state’s Delete Request Opt-out Platform, better known as DROP. The online tool allows California residents to ask registered data brokers to stop selling their personal information without having to contact hundreds of companies individually. Since Jan. 1, about 350,000 Californians have already signed up through the DROP website. Every time someone shops online, streams entertainment, or simply browses the internet, pieces of that person’s digital footprint can be collected, packaged and sold. Tom Kemp, Executive Director of Cal-Privacy, explains how the state agency will enforce compliance with “DROP” requests. “In the digital economy, our personal information is basically oil,” Tom Kemp with Cal Privacy said. Kemp said many consumers don’t realize just how much information is collected whenever they go online. “We oftentimes are the product, our information, our data is the product that people collect, package up into digital dossiers and sell,” Kemp said. He said that information has long been used for targeted advertising. “Historically, that’s been used for targeted advertising. So if you go shopping for red shoes, the red shoes follow you around for the next three weeks,” Kemp said. But Kemp said the information can also become valuable to criminals. “The bad guys, the hackers are leveraging the data from data brokers,” Kemp said. Instead of contacting roughly 600 registered data brokers one by one, Californians can submit a single request through the DROP website. “We’re all gonna hear a giant sucking sound outside of our data being deleted from all these data brokers systems,” Kemp said. He said doing the process manually would be overwhelming. “The alternative is you would have to contact 600 companies and say, please delete my information. And who’s got time for that?” Kemp said. Beginning Aug. 1, registered data brokers have 45 days to process requests submitted through the system. That 45-day processing period repeats for new requests. Companies that fail to comply can face fines of $200 per day for each affected Californian. “And my agency has a dedicated team that will go after to make sure that the will of Californians to take control of their information is taken care of,” a Cal Privacy representative said. Cal Privacy told NBC 7 Responds it has already fined 12 data brokers tens of thousands of dollars each for failing to register in the DROP system. The agency said only California residents are eligible to use DROP, and the tool will not erase all personal information that exists online. Consumers should continue watching for scams and take other steps to protect their personal information. More information about the Delete Request Opt-out Platform is available at https://privacy.ca.gov/drop/. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

headlines.title: Authorities warn of dangerous surf following rescue at Santa Cruz beach
headlines.description: The viral rescue at a Santa Cruz beach on Saturday served as a powerful reminder of why experts say people should swim only at beaches with lifeguards on duty. Thursday night, many headed to Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz. They were having bonfires and others were watching the sunset. Santa Cruz is known for its beautiful beaches, but officials say conditions can change in an instant. “Sometimes you’ll go down to the beach, and you won’t see any waves for a period of time and a whole set will come in,” said State Parks Peace Office Micah Moore. “It’s easy to kind of get lulled into oh this is a tranquil day at the beach not realizing that in the next 5, 10 minutes there may be some pretty big surf.” Santa Cruz Jul 30 Santa Cruz Jul 29 Santa Cruz Jul 28 Those were the conditions last weekend when 16-year-old lifeguard Ryder Williams rescued a 10-year-old boy from the dangerous surf at Seabright Beach. California State Parks says the boy was swept about 15 yards into the ocean before Williams reached him. The 10-year-old was identified as Nathaniel Rai by his father, Sumit Rai, who says he couldn’t believe Williams fought the powerful current to save his son. “And for him to have to grab my son who weighs about 100 pounds when he’s lost consciousness and is limp. Basically deadweight that he’s carrying through those rip currents to bring back to shore is incredibly courageous, brave, heroic. You know he just demonstrated so much resilience and persistence. He never let go of him,” Sumit Rai said. The rescue has been viewed millions of times across the country and even caught the attention of President Donald Trump, who has invited Williams to the White House.

headlines.title: Water main break affecting some Alameda residents
headlines.description: An emergency water main repair disrupted water service for some Alameda residents Friday morning. According to East Bay Municipal Utility District, water service has been interrupted on Pacific Avenue while crews make emergency repairs. The repair work has also closed Webster Street between Buena Vista Avenue and Lincoln Avenue. EBMUD estimates water service will be restored by 4 p.m. Friday.
